issues.item: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Medical Care' is internally inconsistent as written: the label indicates avoidance, but the item text states 'Seeking medical or psychological help,' which is the opposite behavior.

issues.item: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
issues.explanation: 'Overwork' is hard to reconcile with the patient's unemployment status. While unemployed people can keep excessively busy, this wording specifically implies excessive work as a strategy and is therefore clinically implausible for this demographic unless otherwise qualified.

issues.item: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
issues.explanation: These two items imply an active work-based avoidance pattern, which is hard to reconcile with the patient's stated occupation of unemployed. While keeping busy is plausible, 'Overwork' specifically describes excessive working and is therefore clinically incoherent with being unemployed unless supported by another role context that is not present here.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: Checking whether someone is following her suggests a stalking/pursuit-type threat context that is not well aligned with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner, where fear is more typically focused on the partner in domestic spaces rather than unknown followers. With the rest of the profile centered on sleeping alone, vulnerability, restricted safe places, and sleep vigilance, this item pulls toward a different threat pattern.

issues.item: Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
issues.explanation: Bodily reenactment can occur in PTSD, but as selected here it implies a highly embodied, posture-specific trauma memory. Given the other memory items emphasize involuntary intrusion plus active truncation of recall, and the threat profile is oriented toward vigilance and restricted safety rather than reliving a specific assault configuration, this item is less well integrated with the rest of the formulation and self-report pattern.

vignette:
At 68, Ama had been married for many years, but when she spoke about the abuse by her husband, what came through first was not a single incident so much as the atmosphere that had formed around it: evenings when his mood shifted without warning, the way she learned to read the set of his jaw, the smell of damp earth coming in from outside after he had been in the yard, and the sickening knowledge that she was most at risk when she was cornered and emotionally exposed. Some of the worst assaults had followed moments when she was alone with him at night, already undressed for bed, with the house quiet and no one else to hear. The bedroom itself became tied to those moments of helplessness, and even now sleeping alone or anywhere unfamiliar could make her body react as if she were back there, bracing for him to come through the door.

In the years since, Ama had not found that these memories stayed in the past. A faint outdoor smell after rain, the scent of soil from a potted plant, or simply lying down by herself at night could bring the whole scene back without warning. She described the memory as forcing its way in, complete and immediate, before she had time to prepare. Yet once it began, she would also cut it off almost at once, pushing it away before she could fully take in what she had remembered. That left her caught in a painful pattern: she never felt she had really put it to rest, and because the memory could erupt from ordinary things around her, the world felt crowded with reminders she could not fully predict.

Ama had come to organize her days around not letting her mind settle. Since becoming unemployed, she filled the hours with constant tasks—cleaning one room and then another, reorganizing drawers, finding errands to run, keeping the television on in the background—not because these activities gave her pleasure, but because stillness gave the memory room to intrude. When something in her surroundings pulled the abuse into mind, she became even more determined to stay busy and mentally occupied, shifting immediately to a chore, a phone game, or some small practical task. She also noticed herself going along with what other people wanted, even in minor situations, because feeling emotionally vulnerable stirred too much of the same danger; compliance still felt like the quickest way to reduce risk.

What frightened Ama most was how thoroughly the memory had altered her sense of safety. Because it could arrive so suddenly and vividly, she no longer trusted that danger was truly over, even inside her own home. She said there were only a very limited number of places where she could relax at all, and even there the feeling was fragile. At night she struggled to fall asleep because some part of her felt she needed to remain alert, listening to the house and noticing every sound. That constant watchfulness made sleeping alone especially difficult; bedtime was not simply lonely for her, it felt exposing.

Living in that guarded state shaped the way she tried to manage herself. Because she felt on edge even at home, Ama kept herself occupied from morning until late evening, as if movement could hold the fear at bay. She deferred quickly to others, especially when she sensed tension, believing that disagreeing or asserting herself might leave her too exposed. Over time her world had narrowed around a few “safe” places and routines. Anything outside those familiar zones—an overnight stay, an unfamiliar room, even stepping into a garden and catching the smell of fresh soil—was more likely to set her off, and knowing that made her cling harder to the habits she thought protected her.

Those habits, however, had their own cost. The more Ama used busyness and mental distraction to get through the day, the less tolerance she had for quiet moments, and the more easily ordinary sensations stood out as threatening. Because she rushed to cover over any stirrings of memory, a smell from outdoors or the prospect of being alone in bed seemed to hit her with full force each time, as if nothing had ever been processed or finished. Her efforts to stay safe had gradually made her life smaller and more constricted, even within her marriage and home.

By the time she sought help, Ama was exhausted. A recent night spent sleeping by herself had left her pacing the house until dawn, alert to every creak, while the smell of wet dirt from outside had pulled the abuse back so sharply that she could hardly breathe before forcing the image away again. She came to treatment because she could see how trapped she had become by the need to stay busy, agreeable, and watchful. What she feared most was that she would never again feel safe enough to rest. What she hoped, quietly, was to be able to sit still in her own home and know that the past was not about to step into the room.
